title: Ahead of Season
tagline: Twenty-five springs of bird sightings against the temperature each spring actually had — with two birds that never migrate carried along as a lie detector.
blurb: Do migrants arrive earlier in warm springs? This lines up 1.9 million GBIF sighting records — 13 species across Washington, Boston and Atlanta, 2000 to 2024 — against Open-Meteo's ERA5 temperature history for the same ground, and lets you re-sort the twenty-five years by warmth instead of by number to see whether the arrival dates fall into line. Because sightings measure birdwatchers as much as birds, every count is divided by all bird records logged in the same box on the same day, and two year-round residents are run through the identical pipeline as controls: a Northern Cardinal cannot arrive in spring, so whatever shift the method reports for it is the method's own drift. In Washington that drift is −0.13 days/°C and the Baltimore Oriole's 0.65 days per degree stands; in Boston the residents drift +0.70 and the page flags the entire city rather than report it. The Ruby-throated Hummingbird shows nothing anywhere — it winters in Central America and departs on daylength, unable to perceive a warm North American spring, which is the mechanism behind phenological mismatch.
